input.text: When the dictation ends, the app reads the transcript once more before it pastes anything. It splits the text into words, asks the parser which word depends on which, and keeps the original whenever a step is unsure, because a wrong edit costs the user more than a missed one. The parser runs two passes over the same subwords, one for grammar and one for syntax, then a small decoder picks the single best tree with one root. Long dictations are the hard case: a person who talks for a minute about release notes, flaky tests, the staging server in Frankfurt, three pull requests and a coffee order produces far more subwords than a sentence, and the model only reads two hundred and fifty six of them, so the app must notice the overflow and step aside rather than cut the text and guess. Nobody wants a tool that silently drops the end of a thought, least of all someone dictating a careful reply to a colleague late on a Friday afternoon. So the rule is simple to state and dull to test: count first, parse only what fits, and when the count is over, return the text exactly as it came in, with every comma, every repeated word and every half-finished clause still where the speaker left it, so that the person can fix it by hand if they care, and nothing they said has quietly disappeared on the way to the screen.
